messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 26, Daniel had been working on fishing boats long enough that hard weather, heavy gear, and little sleep had once felt ordinary to him. What broke that sense of ordinariness was a period of captivity during which he was tortured. In the first sessions he did not offer a long, orderly account, but the fragments were stark and consistent: being trapped in a confined room, held down in painful positions, and hurt repeatedly until the memory of it lived as much in his body as in words. What stayed with him most sharply was not only the fear, but the humiliation of being completely at someone else’s mercy. Certain sounds from that time seemed to have fused with the experience. A baby crying could cut through him with shocking force because the high, distressed pitch seemed to pull him straight back into that room. Bus rides were almost as bad; being enclosed with strangers, unable to control who came near him or when he could get off, carried the same trapped, exposed feeling. Even moments of emotional openness with his wife could catch him off guard, because feeling vulnerable in any form had come to seem dangerously close to the helplessness he had endured.

In the months afterward, Daniel found that these moments did not just remind him of what had happened in a vague way. When a baby cried in a grocery store or on the dock, the memory hit with a physical immediacy that frightened and infuriated him. He would feel his body tense into the same position he had been forced into during the torture, as if his muscles were reenacting it before he had time to think. The pain returned in the same places where he had been injured, and with it came a surge of intense rage that felt hotter than fear. On buses he sometimes had to grip the seat because it seemed, for a few seconds, that he was no longer in public transport at all but back inside the event, his body already bracing for what came next.

Those memories changed how he moved through the world. Because recall came with such vivid bodily pain and a sense of being pinned again, Daniel began treating ordinary spaces as if danger might erupt in them at any moment. He sat with his back against the wall in diners, waiting rooms, and the galley on the boat, scanning the room so no one could approach from behind. At home he listened for small noises at night, alert for any sound that might mean someone was entering. He noticed tools, knives, hooks, and any heavy object that could be used as a weapon before he noticed much else. He understood that other people did not live like this, but to him it felt like the only sensible response; once his body could be thrown back into the torture so completely, he was certain he could not afford to relax.

That constant watchfulness, though, seemed to make the memories easier to ignite. On the fishing boat, where gaffs, fillet knives, and metal equipment were everywhere, his attention snagged immediately on anything sharp or heavy, and once he was in that state he was more likely to be set off by a crewmate’s raised voice or by hearing a baby cry from a nearby marina. Even bus riding became harder over time because he boarded already braced, already searching for exits and for what could be used against him, and the sense of exposure made every jolt or unexpected sound feel loaded. The more he listened at home for someone entering, the more a harmless creak in the house could leave him rigid, body pulled back into that old position before he fully knew why.

His vigilance also narrowed his life in practical ways. He avoided taking the bus whenever he could, even when it made getting to the harbor harder. On the boat he chose spots where he could see the whole deck, and crewmates had begun to notice that he was edgy if someone came up behind him unexpectedly. His wife saw a different version of the same pattern at home. If a conversation became emotionally close and he felt exposed, he might shut down or pull away, not because he did not want her near but because vulnerability itself had started to feel like a trigger. Afterward he would often be more on edge in the house, checking locks again, listening for sounds, and sleeping in a position that let him face the door.

By the time he came for help, Daniel was exhausted by living as if he were still about to be overpowered. He was angry at how quickly a baby’s cry, a bus, or even the feeling of opening up to his wife could throw him into pain and rage. What frightened him most was how instantly his body seemed to obey the past, and how completely that made the present feel unsafe. He said he wanted to be able to work, ride where he needed to ride, and sit in his own home without listening for an intruder, but underneath that was a more private hope: that he might stop feeling as though helplessness was always one moment away.
